subject: Cognitive Science
title: Fairness and Inequity Aversion
description: A quick, practical guide to Fairness and Inequity Aversion.

hook.text: Give two kids one cookie each—fine. Give one kid two? The other erupts. Fairness instinct is fierce.

buildup.text: By age three, children protest unequal splits. "That's not fair!" is one of the earliest moral claims.

discovery.text: Rejecting less for yourself appears first. Rejecting more than your share appears around age eight.

twist.text: Adults do it too. In the Ultimatum Game, people reject free money if the split feels unfair.

climax.text: Fairness overrides self-interest. People sacrifice personal gain to punish perceived inequality.

punchline.text: We'd rather lose than accept unfairness.

quiz.question: When does disadvantageous inequity aversion first appear?

details.summary: Children develop a strong sense of fairness early, showing inequity aversion by age three or four. They reject unequal distributions even at personal cost. This tendency appears across cultures, suggesting an evolved foundation for cooperation that is refined by social norms.
details.whyItMatters: Fairness is not taught from scratch but built on innate preferences. Understanding its development explains cooperation, protest, and the persistence of equality norms across societies.
takeaways: Inequity aversion appears by age three or four
Children reject unfair offers even at personal cost
Fairness preferences appear across diverse cultures

faq.question: Do children care about fairness for others or just themselves?
faq.answer: Initially children object mainly to disadvantageous inequity, receiving less than others. By around age eight, many also reject advantageous inequity, giving up their own excess to achieve equality. This shift reflects developing concern for others and social reputation.

faq.question: Is the sense of fairness found in other animals?
faq.answer: Capuchin monkeys and chimpanzees reject unequal food rewards, suggesting fairness has evolutionary roots. However, human fairness is far more sophisticated, involving abstract principles, third-party punishment, and culturally variable norms about what counts as fair distribution.
